# How to Use the Sleep Apnea Feature on Galaxy Ring and Galaxy Watch

> **In short:** You can turn on Samsung's Sleep Apnea feature on a compatible Galaxy Watch or Galaxy Ring, wear it while you sleep, and read the results. It looks for signs of moderate to severe sleep apnea. It does not diagnose the condition, so a doctor still makes that call.

If you wake up tired after a full night in bed, or someone has mentioned loud snoring or pauses in your breathing, this guide is for you. By the end, you'll know how to switch on the feature, what it needs from you, and how to read the results without guessing.

## Before you start

- **A compatible Samsung wearable:** a Galaxy Watch or a Galaxy Ring that supports the feature. Samsung's announcement says it is available on both, but not every older model is included.
- **A compatible phone and the Samsung Health app:** the ring and watch pair with the app. Samsung Health is free to download, but check the app for any paid add-on before you use it.
- **About 15 minutes of setup, plus two nights of wearing it.** Your device needs to be charged before bed each night.

## Step 1 — Check that your device and phone are ready

Before you change any settings, confirm the basics. Open the Samsung Health app on your phone and make sure your Galaxy Ring or Watch appears as connected. Look for a device name or a small status line near the top of the screen. If it says disconnected, bring the wearable close to your phone and wait a few seconds.

Next, check your battery. Sleep tracking needs the device to stay on your finger or wrist all night, so charge it to at least half before bed on your first test night. If your phone asks you to update the Samsung Health app or the wearable's software, do it now. Updates can change where settings live, and an old version is the most common reason a feature is missing.

If you don't see your device at all, look for a "Devices" or "Add device" option, usually in the app's main menu. You'll know it worked when your ring or watch shows as connected and its battery level is visible in the app.

## Step 2 — Find the Sleep Apnea feature

Open the Samsung Health Monitor app on your watch, or the health app on your phone, and look for a section about sleep. The feature may appear under a heading like "Sleep" or as its own tile labeled with sleep apnea. On a Galaxy Ring, the setting is more often found inside the Samsung Health app on your phone rather than on the ring itself.

If you can't find it right away, use the search icon (a magnifying glass) if your app has one, and type "sleep apnea." If nothing shows up, the feature may not be available on your model or in your region yet. Samsung's announcement describes it as available on Galaxy Watch and Galaxy Ring, but the exact menu location can change with app updates, so don't worry if the path looks different.

You'll know it worked when you see a screen that mentions sleep apnea and offers a way to turn the feature on or start setup.

## Step 3 — Turn the feature on and follow the setup

Tap the sleep apnea screen's option to start or turn on the feature. Read each screen before you tap "Next" or "Agree," because this is where you'll see what data the feature uses and how it works. Look for a button like "Start," "Next," or "Continue" at the bottom of the screen.

The setup will usually ask you to wear your device during sleep. Samsung's instructions to you may call for wearing it on at least two nights within about 10 days. Read the exact wording on your screen, because this detail is the one you need to get right. If the app shows a countdown or a progress bar, that's the feature collecting your sleep data.

If the setup asks for personal details like your age or sex, answer honestly, since the app needs them to read your signals correctly.

💬 Example: If a text box asks what you're using the feature for, you can type "Checking for signs of sleep apnea during my sleep."

You'll know it worked when the app shows a confirmation that the feature is on, along with a start date or a note about the nights you need to wear your device.

## Step 4 — Wear it correctly for two nights

Put the ring on the finger the app recommends, or fasten the watch snugly on the wrist, about a finger's width above the wrist bone. A loose device can miss readings. Wear it to bed each night and keep it on until you wake up. Charge it during the day so the battery doesn't run out overnight.

Try to sleep your normal way on these nights. Don't force yourself into an unusual position or skip your usual routine just to get a result. The feature looks for patterns in your breathing and body signals, so the more natural your sleep is, the more useful the data becomes.

If the app says it didn't get enough data, that's normal. Keep wearing the device on your next night, and check that it's snug and charged. If you're still stuck after several nights, look for a "Help" or "Support" option in the app.

💬 Example: Set a phone reminder that says "Put on Galaxy Ring before bed" for both of your test nights.

You'll know it worked when the app shows that your nights are being recorded, with each night listed as complete or in progress.

## Step 5 — Read your results and decide what to do next

When your two nights are complete, open the Sleep Apnea result in the app. Look for a summary that says whether signs of moderate to severe sleep apnea were detected, or whether no signs were found. Some results may say the feature couldn't reach a conclusion, which usually means not enough usable data.

Remember what the result is: a screening signal, not a diagnosis. Samsung says the feature points out patterns that may be worth discussing with a doctor. If the app suggests you talk to a doctor, that's a useful next step, and you don't need to wait for a second night of data to make the appointment.

If the wording is confusing, you can copy the result text into an AI chatbot to get a plain-language explanation. Don't use it in place of your doctor, and don't ask it what treatment to take.

💬 Example: "Explain these sleep screening results in plain words, and tell me what questions to ask my doctor: [paste your result text here]."

You'll know it worked when you can say, in one sentence, what the result says and what the next step is.

## Common mistakes

- **Mistake: Taking the result as a diagnosis.** The feature looks for signs. It does not confirm that you have sleep apnea. **Fix:** Use the result as a reason to ask a doctor, and keep any symptoms you've noticed to share.
- **Mistake: Removing the device overnight or letting it die.** Gaps in data can stop the feature from finishing. **Fix:** Charge it every day and keep it on from bedtime to wake-up.
- **Mistake: Wearing it loosely or on the wrong hand or wrist.** Readings can be missed. **Fix:** Use the position the app recommends, and check that it sits snugly before you go to sleep.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** If you're often tired after a full night's sleep, this feature can give you a starting point for a conversation with your doctor, without a lab visit.
- **For your business or work:** If you travel or work long shifts, a wearable can show patterns over several nights, which can help you describe your sleep accurately to a clinician.
- **If you're just getting started:** Begin with the setup and one test night. You don't need to understand every chart before you start.

## Try it now

Open the Samsung Health app on your phone and check that your Galaxy Ring or Watch shows as connected with a charged battery. Then search for "sleep apnea" in the app. If you see the feature, you're ready for your first night.
